What this type of legislation does is deliver us more and more of the control to the centre. We do not allow the boardrooms and owners of the nation any decision-making basis at all, so that decisions can be made in respect of the large and diverse activities of the nation. They have to come crawling in for grants. This will bring an avalanche of requests from the newspaper industry, and it will bring an avalanche of requests for specific rulings to clear up all of the problems in the regulations in this one area.
The hon. member for Edmonton West said that his riding was only serviced by two major dailies. We have two major dailies in my riding but we also have a very hard hitting and very talented weekly newspaper with a Sunday issue, so they are bi-weekly.
That organization has some 700 housewives and school students out delivering that community newspaper on Wednesdays and Sundays. In that community newspaper are fliers from building supply houses, chain stores and grocery stores. These are printed by different presses, the operators of which are trying to eke out a living. The presses are trying to meet good payroll standards throughout the community. That total distribution operation and that bi-weekly operation grew from a mimeographing service within the riding. That very fundamental operation has a solid payroll and a good balance sheet, but it is threatened by this type of legislation, which totally discriminates against it. How can such operations compete? How can the different presses in the community compete when the regulations now give the total cost leverage advantage to Pacific Press, which prints both the Vancouver Sun and the Vancouver Province?
The Liberals, along with their NDP cohorts, continue to label the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada as the party of the multinationals. Let me reply to that by saying that this legislation attacks the small and medium enterprise sector of Canada as nothing I have seen in this House in the last six years attacks it. This delivers unfair advantage to the Thompson and Southam chains. What backroom deal did hon. members opposite make with them to bring in a piece of legislation like this which puts an oppressive cost structure on all weekly and community papers across the land? It is just not fair. There is no equity. There is no fair sharing principle. It does not promote the just society hon. members opposite keep referring to in their rhetoric. Their deeds and their legislation are completely contrary to the principle of fairness.
There is a small business secretariat. There is a Minister of State for Small Businesses, but the small business secretariat is really just a political tool which is totally misused. Sixty-five per cent of the meaningful work created in Canada is created by the small and medium-enterprise sector which, on an individual basis, does less than $20 million a year in sales.
This place just does not represent that community which is not organized and does not have economic clout or economic leverage. I plead with hon. members on the government side to consider these small enterprises which create payrolls. It is true that some of them are marginal payrolls, but if small enterprises could be provided with all the benefits of the big monopolies, they would be monopolies themselves. As it is, some of them grow into very successful enterprises.
This piece of legislation is obviously the result of lobbying by the Thompson and Southam chains. It is obviously the result of the lobby of the Canadian postal service. That service, incidentally, wants to deliver all the mails and wants to change the definition of the word "letter" so that it will include all the electronic media. That service also wants a total monopoly over all communications, and the next thing it will go after will be talk. The government included that in its bill and it took a lot of work in committee to get it to recognize the folly of it. The Post Office is subsidized massively, to the tune of some $500 million or more a year, and now it wants to corral the distribution of advertising and fliers and everything else. At least community newspapers get to the doorsteps at present. There is no guarantee that they will get to the doorsteps through the Post Office, at least on time. Quite often advertised sale is over before the flier arrives through the Post Office. When we get to committee I will plead with hon. members opposite to be prepared to change their minds on that aspect, because the existence of all those independent newspapers is at stake.
With respect to this same issue, it is interesting that a very successful and productive printing enterprise in Vancouver, recently bought out by Southam, now finds itself in the deplorable position of losing all its flier and printing business. It is losing that business even to the Americans. The American multinational accounts in Canada can produce overruns in the United States, pay the sales tax on entry and have a delivered cost less than that of the printing industry in Canada.
When I criticize bureaucrats for creating confused legislation, believe me, there is some justification for it. We have to be out in that rough and tumble world of work to understand the downsides, the triggers and the traps which exist in this type of operation.
I have here a package of regulations with respect to different aspects of this legislation which officials are trying to draft. When I pick up the telephone and talk to departmental officials, they just cringe. They say, "We don't know". That is one aspect about which I feel very strongly, and I hope the government will think seriously about it as we approach discussion at committee stage.
I wish to discuss another inequity. I listened attentively to the Minister of Finance when he was talking about this legislation delivering solutions to anomalies, about different tax levels and about the avoidance which is taking place. Believe me, there is no tax avoidance going on out in the legitimate business world. Businesses do not wildly pay taxes. They hire lawyers and chartered accountants to advise them of the threshold at which they must pay tax. The tax department
February 13, 1981

knows, encourages and puts that game in place. It is a very expensive exercise today to keep from moving into a retroactive tax position because of the lack of clarity in much of the law. I keep saying, please give us back the decision-making base which the government removed in 1972 in the tax legislation produced by the coalition NDP-Liberal government.
We have been slipping. In question period today the Minister of Finance talked about productivity being the key. I am glad he understands that because productivity is the key. It is the key to maintaining our quality of life; it is the key to licking inflation; it is the key to being able to service the world at large and to service the Third World more effectively. The gross national product can only be increased through productivity. However, what oppresses productivity is the complicated nature of the rules under which the wealth-creating sector must operate.
Listen to the howls on this: why tax profits? Profits are a new national resource. Profit is new working capital. The more profits generated in this country, the less we have to borrow abroad. The more profits we create, the bigger the tax revenue because that is what we have been taxing. Let us not tax profits. Let us create that wealth, that Canadian capital, and move to a tax on net cost of value added. This 9 per cent tax is tinker toy stuff, and as long as we have it in the system, that system will get worse and worse and more and more confused.
1 think the Minister of Finance was misleading us when he gave credit to a government member for the reduction in tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent. That is fantastic, but now what is the government doing with this legislation? It is moving the threshold of the tax up another notch and including all the partial manufacturers. I think this is a good move because if we assume value for duty on imported merchandise, which the minister thinks he is addressing with this tax, at 100 per cent of base and use 100 as the base, under the old tax-let us say the pre-January, 1981 base-when there was a 10 per cent duty factor and a 9 per cent federal tax, there was a multiplier of 155. In other words, if the world price was $1, the landed Canadian price would be $1.55. If there was a 17.5 per cent duty rate, it would be 164.5 or $1.64. Under the new budget by moving the threshold up to include the partial manufacturers, 155 becomes 143, so there is now a factor of 1.43, not 1.55.
I am using figures which come from an average of about 930 imported items. With the 17.5 per cent in the duty column, instead of the factor being 1.645 it is now 1.52. So the multiplier of the partial manufacturer has come down.
Let me also put this on the record. When you have a manufacturer's sales tax at the manufacturing level, there is a tremendous multiplier effect on the cost of consumer goods. An item which has the federal sales tax applied at the manufacturing level and which costs $5.50, to round off $5.49, would cost $5 at the retail level if the federal sales tax were not put on it.
Excise Tax
Once again I say that if the aim is to make the country more productive, which the Minister of Finance recognizes as being the key factor in addressing most of the nation's problems, then let him move to the adoption of a net cost value added tax so that the value added at each stage is taxed, and any value added tax which was in any component of the cost can be subtracted in order to get a net value added tax. This would turn the whole matter of production back to the managers. As a result, they would not be buying big cars, putting extra facades on buildings, buying expensive furniture, or travelling first class unnecessarily, and thus building up all these allowable expenses which are charged against profits. The government would be taxing all the waste which exists in the community. Let the government start taxing waste in this land and let it leave profits as an incentive and a new form of wealth, and then let us watch this country grow.
I have another pet theory which should be considered in parallel. We are always looking for answers. I say: let the government get rid of the federal sales tax, which is nothing but inflationary, nothing but a drag and a charge against the payroll package of the work-force in Canada, and let it collect the cost of all social programs from an end-user tax. All of a sudden we will find that the country has turned into one of the most efficient industrialized nations in the world because each and every person will be able to measure what they are demanding of the government in terms of their own wallet or purse.
I do not see any resolution of our problems until we get right back to the basic philosophy of taxation and clean up all these artificial impediments which we have built into our system. I make this appeal once again most sincerely and most constructively.
There is another anomaly in our system which I find very serious. We have just enlarged the threshold and embraced partial manufacturing in the sales tax sector. The words of the Minister of Finance are in Hansard. While he thinks he is making the system more equitable, he is really just reacting to a self-centred lobby, and I know something about that because I lobbied before I came into politics. What has the minister done about the inequities in the definition of small manufacturers? Genstar has ready-mix concrete plants, and is doing a couple of billion dollars in business. It is a Canadian company whose president and senior executives operate out of San Francisco and which owns massive horizontally and vertically integrated subdivisions, using their own concrete products, their own building supply yards, and everything else. It is a beautifully run organization which is getting bigger and bigger. However, in terms of its ready-mix concrete operations, it is classified as a small manufacturer.
Next door to Genstar, or in the same vicinity, within a half mile, there is another organization doing $2 million in sales, which had the idea of buying cement, sand, gravel and different compounds, mixing them together and having the dry product packed for sale. If on a Saturday or on a Sunday I wanted to build a little form for something, I could buy a few bags of this ready-mix, add water to it and pour it in, and I

February 13, 1981
Excise Tax
would feel that I was pretty good at doing something with my own hands. Now the second company has to pay sales tax on the selling price of its product. The smaller company gets the sand, gravel and cement on a tax-exempt basis and has to pay the federal sales tax only on the selling price of the finished bag. The large company, which adds water to the same stuff pays the sales tax on the cost of the cement only, and does not pay it on the sand, the gravel, the administration and the profit. The small company is doing its best, is a good employer, employs good engineers and builds a beautiful little business which is doing $2 million in sales. Genstar is doing $2 billion in sales because it is a ready-mix manufacturer operating under the definition of a small manufacturer, and it pays the sales tax only on the cement. I am told that it does not have to collect the federal sales tax on the selling price of their dry products. It sells their product at 5 per cent below the lowest price the other company can ask.
Let me tell the government that when it brings in legislation with definitions such as the definition for small manufacturer or marginal manufacturer when it causes this type of confusion, it pretty well destroys any chance of improving the productivity of the industrial sector in Canada. What we need in Canada is more manufacturing, because if you move from a primary industry like mining or agriculture into secondary manufacturing where you have the value add, you get a far better multiplier factor in the economic community at large. However, somehow or other we do not think of that in terms of our taxation legislation. We work against ourselves, and then wonder why we are slipping from a very enviable situation in comparison to other industrialized nations, slipping down past all of them to end up in the garbage can.
There is not a nation in the world which that has been as blessed as we are with our hydro and mineral potential, with our nuclear potential in terms of peaceful uses, and with our natural resources. Everything the federal bureaucracy does suppresses the magic of adding to the value of goods and adding to the wealth of the country.
These games played with definitions should, I think, be of serious concern to all of us. I plead with the Minister of Finance, who is not present in the House now, to rid himself of the attitude that it is tax avoidance. It is not. There is no tax avoidance going on in the legitimate business sector. It cannot risk it, it cannot afford it, it does not want it, but there are all kinds of grey areas, so let us clean them up.
Now I should like to move to another small problem which I have been made aware of relating to Clause 4.4 of the bill, and that is the matter of marginal manufacturing. A small company started with one store and a couple of partners. They worked very hard, their wives were involved in the business, and they found the right combination. The company started to grow. The next thing you know, they had a second store, a third store and a fourth store. Then they started to buy Canadian-made products, and rather than go to a packager, they decided to instal their own packaging room and some equipment. They assembled and packaged their products and sent them out to their four stores. Under the new regulations
they can do that and can buy on a federal tax paid basis, provided the product is only used in the store in which it is packaged. They have four other stores, so they must collect the federal sales tax, if they continue this operation, at the retail price. On one Canadian-made product they were paying about 24.9 cents in the way of tax; now they have to pay 47 cents. I could give chapter and verse on a series of products from both American and Canadian manufacturers which causes them anxiety. It is no longer worth having four or five people at work in a packaging room when they own more than one store.
For example, they used to buy large spools of rope. They used to eye splice, cut them off and sell them to length. Now that is partial manufacturing; it is cheaper to have it done either in the United States or elsewhere and purchase it already cut than retaining the four or five jobs in the organization which, by the way, kept people employed year-round even though it was a seasonal activity. It is all disturbed and distorted within the system.
The waste rag business is also affected, because it has such a high degree of unusable products in its operations. I am talking about successful companies, good tax-paying companies, with good payrolls and with 20 or 30 employees. They now find it is hardly worth the effort to stay in the game. They can buy bailed rags from the United States and bring them into Canada. In that way they can stay in the marketplace, whereas if they continue to run their own operations, they are not competitive.
When we design these things, it is important that the Minister of State for Small Businesses be given some muscle and some power rather than just be a political label. He should be instructed to have conference after conference with the different sectors involved so that the correct answers can be found.
I have already given the House what I think is the answer. The net cost value add tax system would turn the country back to the managers. It would eliminate, almost overnight, all the waste in the industrial sector. Hon. members know how conscious I have been of waste in the government sector. The waste in the government sector is nothing compared to the waste which exists at large in this land and out in the business sector because of the basic taxation system.
I should like to return to the remarks made by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance during question period this morning. He said that the issue is our national productivity. We will never resolve that issue, as long as our present taxation system remains in place and as long as the government brings down confusing legislation, such as Bill C-57.
I have dealt with the small business sector. I could go on to the things we do to ourselves in terms of tariffs. For example, another small enterprise in my constituency is concerned about clean air for industrial and grain workers. There are many grain elevators in my constituency. This company has designed a beautiful little pack which goes on one's back. It has an air
February 13, 1981

hose and a mask, and the person wearing it can have forced, clean, filtered air. It requires a little motor with a peculiar little fan. It is a DC portable motor, and it must be brought in from outside. Through its stupid, idiotic definitions in terms of tariff items, the government forces the company to pay an excise duty and federal sales tax on the motor as it comes in, when they should be paying federal sales tax on the whole thing. They should be able to buy that motor and fan duty and tax free, so that the product can remain of Canadian manufacture. Because of the way that tariff item reads now, they should go down to the United States to have that item manufactured, then bring it into the country on a fully-finished basis. The things we do to ourselves, which affect people who have not had the background experience of the rough and tumble of the work world, are totally negative.
Another tariff item that troubles people is the peculiar light dentists use when they are examining mouths. If it is attached to a dental chair, it comes into the country duty free. If it is unattached, the dentists must pay duty on it. Why? They can buy the light, send it to Italy to be attached to a chair, and then it can be brought in duty free. But, if they want to buy the light and attach it to something made in Canada, they must pay duty on it. I could refer to example after example of negative traps and tricks which interfere with the Canadian value add.
I realize time is precious and one of my colleagues wants to say a few words. In conclusion, I should like to indicate that our very complex tax act is interfering with the productivity we so desperately need in the country. We need to return to a simple tax act. We need to return to an incentive system where the minds and brains of people are sparked and given a vitamin shot. We need to return the decision-making base to the managers and boardrooms of the country instead of leaving it in the halls of the big buildings in Ottawa. We should not tax profits; we should tax net value add, which I will explain in another speech some time. That would allow us to manage and to tax costs and would wring out the waste in the land. We should be given legislation which defines the behaviour expected of the business community. We should not structure the business community because that adds burden upon burden and confusion upon confusion for the creative sector. We should think about bringing in legislation which provides employee ownership plans, the same kind of tax haven which has been given in retirement savings plans. Then we should spread the ownership of the industry in the private, small and medium-enterprise sectors, and the ownership of larger corporations among the employees under some kind of a tax-exempt plan.
For goodness' sake, we should take the power to give research and development grants away from the bureaucracy. We should strengthen research in the universities so that we will have qualified people to send out to fill the positions and the need in our industries. We should include an incremental incentive for the spending of research dollars in the industry; then we could resolve the research and development dilemma in the country.

I have debated this issue for hours in previous Parliaments. For goodness sake, let hon. members hear that debate and share the decision-making base. We talk about sharing. The decision-making base should be shared among the people taking the risk, not in the halls where people say, "That tax point is ours; we can spend it more wisely than you can, dummy." That is not the proper attitude, it is not the way to resolve the problems in the land.
I will sit down now, and I hope the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) might be recognized next.

Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). 1 think he will realize it was a great tragedy for Canada and the people of the country that he did not have an opportunity, as minister responsible for small business, to bring this type of philosophy into the tax laws of this nation.

My remarks will be brief in order to allow the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) to have the floor. On this particular occasion I will only deal with a part of this bill primarily because it is an example of where the government has changed its mind and has done something as the result of advice from Members of Parliament. 1 would like to see that attitude continue in committee.
I am talking about a very historic matter in Canadian political history. According to this excise tax legislation, it is now legal to have an alcoholic still. If anyone knows the history of alcohol in this country, what I have just said immediately becomes significant. This question of the overconsumption of alcohol for drinking purposes runs through our political history. Because of the tremendous concern over this problem, we have put the damper on individuals owning their own alcoholic still.
Alcoholic distillation is an ancient process which many people have used to reproduce the waste of the products in the country around them for many purposes in addition to drinking. There is a little section on definitions in this bill. What the government has done to remove the great penalties found in the existing legislation is to call alcohol, "denatured spirits", rather than call it "denatured alcohol".
Canadians will soon realize that they have finally received some freedom. As long as they remember to call the product "denatured spirits" they will not be stepping on the toes of the police. Over the years many hon. members have tried to point out that there is more wealth in the waste in our system than there is in the product. I have mentioned this point in the House so many times that the nickname I was given when I first came here was Johnny Appleseed, because I kept trying to say that there is more money in trees than in grass.

Oh, no, there isn't.

speechtext:
I am not
talking about the type of grass to which the hon. member is referring; I am referring to cereal grains. The question of the utilization of waste is very important to the economics of Canada. Half of our fishing production is waste. A large proportion of our agricultural production is waste. Sixty per cent of our forestry production is waste. This is all because we are not using the knowledge which is there, to utilize this for waste in the interests of the people and the country.
Alcoholic stills might seem like a small item, but experts calculate that with the privilege of having stills and using the waste of the farm, fishery and other industries-even the housewife could use it if she wants-we could produce 3 per cent to 5 per cent of the total energy needs of this nation, which run into billions of dollars. I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) whom I accused in one of my earlier speeches of having zigged when he should have zagged. In this case he did zig when he should have zigged!
This change was in the Crosbie budget. It also included a tax deduction for people who paid wages to their spouses; a proposal that the cost of renewable energy hardware could be written-off in two years and a proposal for Small Business Development Bonds which would have cut interest rates just about in half. I could mention a couple of other points, but I am talking about stills. As long as the producer is careful to call the product spirits instead of alcohol, this legislation will get him off the hook and allow him to own a still. I have not seen too many headlines on this matter, but it makes the farmers dance in their yards.
Instead of brewing their alcohol out in the bush or in the bluffs, they can now brew it in their home, pay the wife to watch it-which is tax deductible-and produce $4,000 to $5,000 worth of alcohol. That was the intent of the Crosbie budget. This legislation, however, has a limitation, which is that these spirits can only be used for experimental purposes and only for fuel by the individual.
It will cost between $6,000 and $10,000 to build an efficient still to handle such waste products as frozen grains, certain vegetables and the list of 60 or 70 plants which can be put through a still to make spirits. I suggest to the government that it broaden these regulations and add a clause to allow the farmer or individual who owns the still-in addition to using the spirit for his tractor, car, or truck, keeping the motor clean and preventing wear and tear-to sell his legitimate surplus to a legitimate gasoline station, even Petro-Canada. The oil company which buys this surplus spirit would be able to sell it to customers along the highway. If gasohol is sold with a 10 per cent to 20 per cent mix and the price remains the same, many car operators will use it exclusively because it enables the car to run two to three times longer. Instead of disposing of the car at 75,000 or 100,000 miles, it will now run for 200,000 miles or 300,000 miles.
If an amendment is introduced which will allow that individual who owns this still to sell his surplus, which will be controlled through licence and checked by the R.CMP, to a legitimate gasoline filling station, which will keep records of
what is received and what is sold, then the operation will be economical for the farmer and will warrant the price of from $6,000 to $10,000 for a still. A still operator must put through a certain amount of volume to make it pay, because the price of alcohol is only $2 to $3 per gallon.
Beside the economic advantages of allowing the individual to sell a surplus up to a certain amount, say 2,500 gallons, which would cover the great majority I am sure, then the farmer will produce 3 per cent to 5 per cent of our total energy requirement from a renewable resource, namely, waste. The product will add to the life of the motors of the cars and, socially, it will stop the bootlegging. The farmer cannot be expected to throw away his surplus spirits. Since we are dealing with denatured alcohol which cannot be consumed, the farmer will give it to his friends, or, in some cases, peddle it, under the table. This will mean the continuation of what has been going on for the past 60 years to 80 years with the Mounted Police patrolling the roads every night, watching for smoke and trying to smell mash.
People live in an atmosphere of expecting that sooner or later they will be going to jail. Since the government has gone so far as to say the producer can use it for his own use, it should now make it legitimate by saying he can sell his surplus to a legitimate filling station operator. This is the case in 36 states of the United States. With our farmers living just across the road from American farmers who have these opportunities,
I think it is important that we match them. This would not reduce or increase the revenue to the tax collector at all. It would solve a social problem, produce new wealth, fight inflation and make the cars and engines last longer. I think it is a measure which could easily be put in place.
I would now like to talk about the human aspect of this measure. The place where it would do the most good is in the areas of Canada where it is also most needed. I think of Cape Breton where the minister comes from. If there is any part of the world which needs more money it is Cape Breton. The opportunity is available to them, with their fish and farm combination, to make an extra $5,000 a year very easily, working along with their present jobs, utilizing waste, serving their country and making the engines of the district last longer.
I am also reminded of the vast regions of Quebec which are away from cities, northern Ontario, the prairies, B.C., even the Yukon and Northwest Territories. It would be possible to utilize waste in those areas by making this spirit still available up to economic levels where farmers could use it without abusing it. I think the limit should be set at 2,500 gallons, which I know was the figure to be used in the regulations under the previous administration. By using a simple device like this the worry would be taken off the RCMP, the farmer could sleep at night without worrying and, above all, we could make use of the wealth of this nation in a very constructive way.

I will conclude by congratulating the minister for accepting this proposal from the Crosbie budget. He should go whole hog and take advantage of the work that the Department of Agriculture has done, not only through the speeches of the minister but in the pamphlets which have been prepared to explain the operation of a still, its dangers and its good points. This information should be sent out to several hundred thousand people who live on the land, who work in the bush, who are on the farms and beside the sea. It would take a year or so to put a still of the size I am talking about into operation. More progress could be achieved by broadening the legislation in the way I suggest.
I would like to thank the House, Mr. Speaker, for letting me take this time to talk about such an historic occasion-when stills finally became legal in our country.

Of course. I also thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I do so not only for the time allowed me to participate in this debate but for arranging that this subject be referred to the standing committee. To me that is very important.
I would like to begin my remarks by saying that I consider this legislation the most significant of all legislation necessary to implement the National Energy Program launched by the October 28 budget. I say that because it offends and contradicts the very roots and fundamental concepts of Alberta and Saskatchewan's entry into confederation in 1905 and the subsequent transfer of our natural resources in 1930.
My remarks will deal almost entirely with the implications of this bill on our natural gas resources and the total natural gas industry. These remarks will also be appropriate for the companion tax provisions, that is, the petroleum and gas revenue tax or the 8 per cent wellhead tax.
Excise Tax
Natural gas in Alberta, especially in southern Alberta, is very much a part of our heritage. It is part of our history from our very beginning. Natural gas is inextricably a part of our survival of the drought and depression of the 1930s and the ten year adjustment period following. That 20-year period of our history was, in reality, a lost generation and the memories and scars are still evident. Our natural gas history began about 100 years ago when the first gas wells were drilled in the communities of Medicine Hat, Alderson and Bow Island. They were drilled by a Mr. J. A. Grant, who came out west from Sarnia, Ontario.
After that early beginning, Medicine Hat quickly developed its own complete utility system for heating, electric power generation and even street lighting. Even in my day, as a schoolboy, I can remember the town's natural gas street lights which were never turned off because gas was so plentiful. In those early days the city regularly flared a gas well at the CPR station to entertain visiting dignitaries, including Rudyard Kipling, who was sufficiently impressed as to observe that surely Medicine Hat had all hell for a basement.
Those early gas wells were drilled with cable tools and walking beam rigs. The drilling derricks were built from 2x12 planking and took months to build. The drilling operations took years, very often with shutdown periods while the owners went off to arrange more money to carry on the operation. I can well remember one such well about 15 miles from our ranch which carried on for years and eventually made a big strike. This caused great enjoyment at first and then total disappointment followed because gas had been struck and not oil. Other than heating a caretaker's shack, that particular well was of no use, since there was no market for the gas. The enormous derrick eventually blew down and was used as firewood by neighbouring farmers. The well burned for several years before it was eventually sealed off by a new conservation authority. All of this took place about 50 years ago, but I can remember it vividly.
I have said that natural gas resources are part of our heritage. The modern-day development of the total natural gas industry began in the late 1930s and throughout the 1940s. Today's enormous gas industry, including gas wells, pipelines, petrochemical plants, compression stations and a vast array of natural gas service industries all began when a former Alberta premier, Ernest C. Manning, now Senator Manning, passed the necessary Alberta legislation to allow the export of natural gas and oil in 1949. That provision was applicable across provincial borders as well as the United States border.
The total natural gas development was a significant factor in the long, slow recovery following the lost generation about which I spoke. This was particularly so in the agricultural sector of southern Alberta. I would say it was at least a partial compensation for those drought years.
I am referring to gas development, of course. For the first time in our history as a province we were able to begin catching up to other parts of the prairies, which do not have

February 13, 1981
Excise Tax
our severe semi-arid climate, and this thanks to the newly developed part of our natural gas heritage.
Today, with this proposed legislation, all of this Alberta natural gas heritage, this Alberta way of life, is severely threatened in two ways; first, as to the constitutional legality as a result of this legislation, and second, as to the very obvious and crippling implications to come on the implementation of this act and the related petroleum and gas revenue tax.
The Alberta Court of Appeal has already heard the submission of the governments of Alberta and Canada on this issue. Its decision has not yet been brought down. Alberta is claiming that the federal government has no right to tax our natural gas for two fundamental reasons. First, Section 125 of the British North America Act says it all in just 15 words. It reads: "No lands or property belonging to Canada or any province shall be liable to taxation." Second, natural resources in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba were formally and legally transferred from the federal government in 1930 to the prairie provinces. I emphasize most emphatically that this 1930 transfer means that in those provinces we own those natural resources. Surely it takes precedence over the sweetheart deal between the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) which referred to "management and control" subject to a federal override.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: That was an NDP sell-out.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
That deal was, of course, made in the constitutional debate.
The Alberta argument was countered by federal lawyers who insisted that this position only applies to resources still in the ground and that all commodities become liable to taxation once they are in transit. Where do we stop with this argument? Our agricultural soils are a natural resource. Should a product of those soils, such as wheat, become taxable in transit? What about the case of our hydro potential from our rivers or from gas-fired electrical energy? Should this energy and end product become taxable in electrical transmission systems? The implications here are staggering, since it should surely include Ontario and Quebec hydro. It must surely be apparent now in the prolonged constitutional debate that Alberta is chiefly concerned about the complete takeover of Alberta's resources, by way of a referendum or by any other means. This is a very real concern in Alberta now.
I would now like to give some indication of the impact this legislation will have dealing with natural gas only. My remarks apply primarily to southern Alberta, but they do cover a much wider area as well. My city of Medicine Hat has developed and owned all of its own utilities beginning about 100 years ago. It includes electrical utilities generated from natural gas. Medicine Hat's population, including nearby Redcliff, is about 40,000. A large greenhouse industry faces staggering cost increases. Nine separate greenhouse operations face increases of 100 per cent, 102 per cent, 106 per cent, 166 per cent and 200 per cent respectively. These costs are for this excise tax only. They do not include the 8 per cent wellhead tax. A typical home owner in Medicine Hat using about 15 Mcf per
month is now paying 50 per cent more. A senior citizen's home is paying 40 per cent more. The absolute dollar impact on the total city gas consumption is S6.5 million or about $18,000 a day. This is for the first incremental stage only.
I come now to the commercial uses in the city. A co-op shopping centre has an increase in gas costs of 77 per cent and an increase of 16.5 per cent for electrical costs. The gas costs for our district hospital, which services the whole rural community, have increased 106 per cent. Its electrical bill is up 23 per cent. All residential, commercial and industrial electrical costs have increases ranging from 13 per cent to 26 per cent. Again, these cost increments do not reflect the 8 per cent wellhead tax or the present very high interest rates. Easily the most severe impact of the gas cost increases will be felt by our senior citizens, especially those farmers, mostly from Saskatchewan, who seem to enjoy retirement in Medicine Hat with the comforts of natural gas.
The town of Brooks has already suffered more severely than Medicine Hat. Brooks has a population of 9,000 and has grown very quickly as a result of the oil and gas industry. Some 25 specialized service industries are based at Brooks and have already experienced severe cutbacks. There are another 175 businesses directly related to the oil and gas industries. Brooks expects a 30 per cent to 35 per cent reduction in its business activity, because of the National Energy Program, most of it as a result of the natural gas section within that policy. The number of drilling rigs in the Brooks area has already decreased from 70 to 50. Quite recently, and I find this most interesting, two rigs have left for Australia. The balance of this local reduction in drilling rigs has either moved to the United States or they have shut down. In the Brooks service area, less than 10 per cent of the companies have any affiliation with multinationals. More than 70 per cent of supplies, manufactured goods, fabricated goods and vehicles originate right here in central Canada.
I want to say a word or two about the Federation of Alberta Gas Co-ops Ltd. I am sure members of all parties will remember the 18-member board of directors of this rural, provincewide national gas consumer group which visited members of Parliament and other groups about two weeks ago. This federation is made up of 77 user-member gas co-ops, five county-owned utilities and other private gas utilities throughout Alberta. These 85 user-member-owned utilities provide over
40,000	natural gas services to over 140,000 rural people with a 40,000-mile distribution system. Their brief to all members of Parliament documents in some detail their concerns about this new legislation. They point out that 85 per cent of Alberta's rural population have homes which are heated by natural gas. They have, justifiably, concerns about the impact of fertilizer costs because, of course, natural gas is a major input component of commercial fertilizers. These gas co-ops have advanced a very sensible suggestion, namely, that the 30-day pay period for the tax be extended to 90 days.
All of the various cities, towns, rural associations and many others have grave concerns and misgivings about this legislation and the companion petroleum and gas revenue tax. I can
February 13, 1981

certainly understand and appreciate these concerns. A very wide selection of both gas producers and consumers should be encouraged to appear before the standing committee when the bill is sent there. That is the very least the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) can arrange. It is my understanding that this is the government's intention.
As I indicated earlier, we in southern Alberta consider our natural gas resource as part of our 100-year heritage. It would be difficult to place a monetary value on this aspect of our gas heritage resource. I can only add that Alberta's other financial Heritage Trust fund-and most of you know what I am referring to-pales in insignificance in comparison to our natural gas heritage resource.

subtopic: HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS POWERS OF COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE
HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS POWERS OF COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE
speechtext:
That the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs be empowered to examine, inquire into and report from time to time appropriate measures for the prevention, identification and treatment of abused persons involved in interfamily violence and in particular, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, to address the issue of battered wives and dependants and for such other measures in the same matter as the committee may consider desirable.
He said: Mr. Speaker, a few years ago this House took a giant stride forward in recognizing and coming to grips with the battered child syndrome. The House Standing Committee
Family Violence
on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs conducted an in-depth study involving more than 300 different authorities into the question of child abuse which is a broad continuum stretching from deprivation and child neglect on the one hand to the physical battery of children on the other.
The line of demarcation between federal and provincial jurisdictions was traced, responsibilities of parties identified and sound recommendations for remedial action were made. Today I want to ask the House to consider a similar measure related to the broader spectrum of family violence and interfamily violence.
Inasmuch as we have focused the light of truth on the social and legal problems related to child battery, I think the time has long past when spouse battering should come out of the closet and we should attempt to identify the basic elements and seek remedies.
The excellent report on this subject by the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, published just one year ago, interprets the statistics, puts to rest some old myths, identifies some causative dynamics, takes a realistic look at what is being done and addresses the question of what remains to be done.
The facts speak for themselves. Battering is rarely a onetime occurrence. The Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women reports that one in ten Canadian women are battered and most of them have nowhere to go for help, and those who seek help face high legal and financial barriers.
There is no geographical, financial, educational or class exclusion to the perpetrators of this form of violence. We know that 50 per cent of the husbands of battered women interviewed by transition houses were beaten as children, compared to about one third of the women. We know that 55 per cent of the husbands were working; that the one transition house which asked whether the mate had a criminal record found that 34 per cent did, and that the husband's educational level tended to be, like his wife's, about grade 11.
It bears repeating that these statistics should not be interpreted as statistics on battered wives across Canada. They are statistics on one group of battered wives who went to transition houses for help in 1978.
This does not reduce the impact or the validity of the statistics. Still they must not be used to conclude that middle or upper-class women are rarely battered. Many transition house workers spoke of the web of silence around middle and upper-class wife battering. The information on middle-class wife battering comes primarily from doctors, lawyers, police and social workers who refer women to transition houses, and also for middle-class women who may phone for advice but do not stay in the house. These reports and the statistics confirm the conviction that wife battering is just as common in middle and upper-class homes.
Wife beating has been condoned throughout history. The Canadian advisory council report refers to the first known written laws, thought to date from about 2500 B.C., which proclaimed that the name of any woman who verbally abused

February 13, 1981
Family Violence
her husband was to be engraved on a brick which was then to be used to bash out her teeth.
Wife beating and wife killing were recognized rights of men in Greek and Roman societies. Throughout the middle ages wife beating was openly encouraged and the Renaissance brought no relief to women. The eighteenth and nineteenth centuries also spawned laws that proclaimed man's right to abuse his wife. British law textbooks in the nineteenth century still stated that the husband had, by law, power and dominion over his wife and could beat her, but-and here we have the emergence of the first delicate sense of justice in the exception, which states-"but not in a cruel or violent manner".
What are the causes of wife battering? Alcohol, mental illness, natural male aggression, violence passed on from one generation to the next, status imbalance, alienation and the inability to communicate, stress-social pathology?
Alcohol is in fact present in a large number of cases of wife abuse and although it may be a facilitator, its role as a causal factor may be more prominent in the social use of alcohol to legitimize violence and to reinforce a certain image of family relationships.
Wife battering is too widespread to be explained primarily by mental illness. There are many theories and there are many commentaries on the theories, but perhaps the time has come for us to look for cause in the wider society rather than in the individual or the particular family. Wife battering is not a modern phenomenon, and there are many facilitators like alienation, alcohol, status imbalance, stress and social pathology.
Any examination of the phenomenon of family violence has got to take a look at the family as an institution and the relationships between not the individuals, but the individual roles within the family that perpetuate this form of violence; indeed the institution of the family has to be explored in the context of legal and medical institutions against the background of wife battering and family violence in the privacy of the marital home.
The Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women has made some excellent recommendations for a series of changes to the Canada Assistance Plan, a federal-provincial cost sharing arrangement for social services, that would help battered wives. The council recommended modifications to provide more funds for transition houses for battered women, to base a needs test applied to the women on their own income rather than their husband's income, and to loosen residency roles because the houses do not exist in every community. The council recommended an emphasis in the justice system on wife battering as a serious criminal offence.
I believe that as parliamentarians we should address these recommendations and we should also invite the interdepartmental committee of senior civil servants who have been looking at this problem to share their thoughts with us.
The role of family violence and the law, medical response, the role of social agencies, the inevitable cycle of despondency and frustration, marriages outside the law, all invite study.
Transition houses, police crisis intervention, police training programs, United Way initiatives, legal initiatives in Canada, are all indicators of what can be done to help alleviate a serious critical and unjust situation.
In my personal view the question of long-range prevention, and an inventory of emergency services and support services along with legal reforms, are high priorities for early action. What I have been describing for the past few minutes is not one problem, it is many problems; complex problems, interwoven problems and problems that have been with us since the emergence of civilization. The fact that it has existed for centuries is no excuse for one more day's delay. Last year an estimated 50,000 Canadian women were battered, some of them to death. How much longer do we have to wait before we take action?
This is not a political question, it knows no bounds of race, creed, religion or politics. We have before us a human problem and I believe that we have accumulated the intelligence, the desire and the ability to finally do something about it. In the name of humanity, Mr. Speaker, I urge this House to pass my resolution so we can take one giant step forward on the high road to a just and compassionate society.

subtopic: HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS POWERS OF COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased and honoured to have the opportunity to speak to the motion brought to the House by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie). I think it is an excellent motion.
When one reflects for a moment or two that homes across Canada can be the showcase of the best of human relations, one must also recognize that the worst of human relations can also be present there. As the hon. member has articulated very clearly and thoroughly in his presentation, they can be very dangerous places.
We are discussing a topic which has touched in one way or another the lives of all of us in the House. I would be surprised if everyone here did not know of someone who, at sometime in his or her life, had not been affected by family violence in one form or another, be it child abuse, wife battering, or sexual assaults. It is interesting to note that nearly half of the rape victims in Canada are either married or living common law. We are not talking about a situation involving strangers but rather something close to the family unit.
In the motion put forth by the hon. member he mentioned family violence relating to interfamily squabbles. I think the term would be "intra", within the family, as opposed to violence between families. It is fair to say that wives and children are the two groups we are primarily concerned about this afternoon. They are two groups that do not really have a voice and they are powerless in Canadian society. They do not have a lobby group in Ottawa and consequently more responsibility falls on our shoulders to raise this issue in the public consciousness and to take steps in the direction we are taking today. The hon. member mentioned a number of causes of
February 13, 1981

family violence I should like to add one more to the very thorough list presented and that is, unemployment.
I think it is recognized now that unemployment results in a whole host of social costs to Canadians, costs such as increased suicides, alcoholism, hospitalization of one kind or another, prison terms, delinquency and, indeed, family violence. During periods of unemployment a person loses the ability to provide for a family, loses self-esteem, becomes frustrated and despondent. This often results in violence against other persons, including children and wives. At the moment, in Canada, family violence is a growing concern as is our concern about unemployment, the two being not causal but certainly related.
I listened with interest when the hon. member for York-Sunbury indicated that family violence cuts across all lines of society. It is not relegated to any particular sector of society. It is not an upper-class or a lower-class phenomenon but is found in all walks of life. One in ten wives is battered. Recently I read that in the United States there is a wife abuse in 60 per cent of all marriages. A recent study estimated that in metropolitan Toronto about 50,000 wives could be considered battered in one way or another.
In Vancouver, over an 18-month period, 800 wives came forward as victims of serious wife battering and physical abuse. The sad thing is that there is very little research on this topic in Canada or elsewhere. The study previously mentioned by the hon. member is one of the major studies, and it is one of the very few which exists on this topic. It is something we often take for granted. I would like to remind members of the House of the phrase "rule of thumb" which is one we have all heard and perhaps used ourselves. When we look at the origin of that term, it goes back to the old English common law when it was appropriate to beat your wife as long as it was for a good reason. You could not beat your wife with a stick thicker than your thumb. In other words, the "rule of thumb". When we consider the origin of that term we realize this problem has been around for some time.
Canadian statistics indicate that somewhere between 200,000 and 225,000 children per million feel the results of child abuse. I think by all accounts that is a very conservative statistic. The frequency and amount of child abuse in our society today is an increasing phenomenon and a very serious one. It is much greater than indicated by statistics. "Spare the rod, spoil the child" is a statement which is still heard very much within Canadian society today.
I read a 1977 task force study carried out in the province of Ontario which found that within the provincial context, very serious staff hampered the ability to deal with family violence. There are very serious shortages of resources and agencies to deal with this. I am certain Ontario is not unique in this respect. To begin to appreciate the seriousness of this problem, we find, looking at the logs of police work, depending on the municipality or the area of Canada involved, that between 10 per cent and 30 per cent of police calls have to deal with family disputes and family violence. One could almost say it has become a national pastime for many Canadians to beat their children or a husband, his wife. It is not a very pleasant
Family Violence
thing to have to say. We must consider the pain, embarrassment and shame which result.
Obviously, we must increase community services, increase community resources and support systems. Transition homes of one kind or another are needed. Certainly we need large numbers of counsellors to deal in a professional way with this very serious problem. There is dearth of crisis centres across Canada to deal with family violence, child abuse, wife battering and rape. The latest statistic I have been able to obtain indicates that only 35 rape crisis centres exist across the country. When we consider the large metropolitan areas, that statistic is a poor implication of our concern as a society with these very serious problems.
The hon. member indicated the need for police training. There is a need for a new consciousness and a new awareness of that kind of training in our policy forces. Right now I suspect that a policeman is rather hesitant or reluctant to become involved in family violence and family disputes and will tend to avoid that kind of conflict instead of intervening.
With respect to the whole matter of our legal system, we certainly need to have laws with teeth in them and which show some sensitivity to this problem. I think it would be fair to say, as a generalization at least, that our legal system is rather "macho" in nature, especially when we think of the lawyers and judges within the system. It is a male-dominated system and rather macho in interpretation, which certainly does not result in sensitivity to this very crucial question.
There is also the matter of parenting skills. One assumption we in society make is that anyone is capable of raising a family. Our school system does not particularly reflect a concern regarding the development of parenting skills. 1 think we are dealing with perhaps one of the most sensitive of human relations, the raising of children. We are also dealing with the liaison between a husband and a wife. Yet no training in parental skills is really introduced in society. It is assumed that we all know inherently or have some innate ability. All of us here would certainly agree that that is not necessarily the case.
Finally, with respect to a public awareness program, there should be more of the kind of thing which is occurring here today. Members of Parliament are speaking out and recognizing the seriousness of this issue in Canadian society. The more the public is aware of the needs these crisis situations create, the more likely it is that solutions will be found.
In my community of Kamloops there is often a hesitation to accept a transition home, a halfway house or a transition home for young children with problems of one kind or another in the community. This public reaction is almost predictable. With public awareness and a more sensitive attitude toward this serious situation, the natural knee-jerk negative response would not be as common as we find it today.
It is with a great deal of pleasure that I say that our party will certainly endorse this motion. I congratulate the hon.

February 13, 1981
Family Violence
member for bringing it to the floor of the House. We look forward to action and results emanating from this motion.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Celine Hervieux-Payette (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS POWERS OF COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to thank the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) for presenting this motion. I would like to express my full support for the motion.

All the hon. members in the House today are certainly aware that this government has committed itself to finding solutions to the problem of family violence, especially the odious issue of wife battering and child abuse, as I believe that one seldom occurs without the other. Recently, the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women published a brochure entitled The Battered Wife in Canada, an Anonymous and Silent Victim. I hope that this brochure can be distributed in our institutions throughout the country because I believe that the major problem in this regard is one of ignorance and silence and the fact that the population is kept in the dark or would prefer not to hear about it.
However, I would like to point out some of the initiatives taken by our government. First of all, since the Speech from the Throne, an inter-departmental committee including representatives from the Council on the Status of Women, from the Department of Justice, from the Department of the Solicitor General and from the Department of National Health and Welfare has undertaken a study on family violence and particularly on the problem of battered wives. Each of the three line departments represented has sponsored projects and taken certain initiatives: for instance, the Department of Justice has financed conferences, public assemblies and legal information brochures, as well as experimental projects to help the victims; the Department of the Solicitor General of Canada has offered a training program to the RCMP in the area of family violence and has also financed conferences and workshops, as well as a vast research and experimentation program to improve the response of the legislators to the plague of family violence; third, the Department of National Health and Welfare has now under way 40 research and experimentation projects related to family violence including transition houses. These programs are ongoing and I am convinced that others will be implemented.
Nevertheless, if we agree to a reference of this issue to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, it is because of the existence of a real need which was readily identified by the interdepartmental committee but which to a great extent still remains without an answer. I wish to emphasize the need to bring this issue to the attention of the public and to provoke and sustain the interest of Canadian men and women as well as their desire to solve this problem. Whoever abuses a member of our society is committing a crime against society as a whole.
This is not interfering in family relations, whether we are talking about women or children. Our society already recognizes as its duty to protect children, but not yet unfortunately in the case of battered wives. We must, through all available means, give protection to all abused persons, women being by far the largest in number. And I do not hesitate to add, Mr. Speaker, that this is probably the most odious-most often committed and yet the most rarely reported crime in Canada at this time.
The study of the matter will not be easy because it fills one with horror and the interest it attracts is not only a desire for information. One can stay awake all night fuming with rage just thinking about something like this. Until now, women's organizations alone have been trying to really deal with this. I am grateful that two of my male colleagues have agreed to consider the matter and are prepared to deal with it. Even though women's groups are still at the consciousness-raising level, I think we must go one step further and see how we could deal with the situation and solve the problem.
We must concentrate on identifying and treating the battered wives who are a product of family violence. For the time being we would only be wasting time in searching for causes without really helping the half million battered women in Canada, and that I think is a conservative estimate. We must help these women now, Mr. Speaker, without regard for the number of their injuries, the level of socially accepted violence or the frequency of the incidents, because from the victims' point of view, these situations are unacceptable. Mr. Speaker, it is with great sincerity that I support this motion and recommend that it be implemented as soon as possible by the interdepartmental committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS POWERS OF COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as much as we all would like to think of Canada as one of the more enlightened countries in the world, a country where law and order is well established and a country where the human rights of each and every individual is respected by all others, I am sad to say that such is not always the case.
The resolution introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie), this afternoon focuses on one of the ongoing tragedies in Canadian society, and that is violence within the family. It is a problem which cries out for government action but, more than that, it demands of each and every Member of Parliament that we have a better awareness and a much greater willingness to tackle the problem than we have shown in the past.
Violence is always tragic, but violence within the family is even more so, for the victims are so vulnerable and so defenceless. They are preyed upon by the very people to whom they give their trust and on whom they depend. Family violence is far more widespread than reported cases indicate. According to a study done by the University of Windsor, there are ten unreported cases for every case reported. There are ten unreported cases of battered wives to every reported case.
February 13, 1981

This is why family violence is so difficult to combat. It goes on in the privacy of the home and is very often hidden by the victim in order to protect the very thing that has turned against him or her-the family.
Now I want to focus very briefly, as others have, on one aspect of family violence, that is, wife battering. That is the subject we have been discussing this afternoon. All forms of violence are horrifying, as the hon. member for Montreal-Mer-cier (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette) said, but wife battering has not received the attention or concern that its seriousness merits. For example, the laws concerning child abuse in Canada are far ahead of those regarding wife battering. It is now mandatory for citizens outside the family to report known cases of child abuse, but this is not the case in the abuse of wives. Indeed, most provinces, sir, a woman still cannot sue her husband for damages because those damages have been caused by an assault committed during marriage.
The rape of a woman by her husband is not yet a criminal offence. I know that legislation is about to come before us, but I would like to see it brought forward much more quickly for second reading. It was only in 1968, 12 years ago, Mr. Speaker, that severe physical abuse became valid grounds even for divorce in Canada.
The problem of wife beating is real and it is very serious. Most Canadians have no idea just how widespread it is. Of all the forms of family violence, and there are many, three quarters of the hundreds of thousands of cases which take place involve wife beating.
In 1978, just two years ago, it was estimated that some
500,000	or half a million, Canadian women were beaten by their husbands or their live-in companions. That is one in every ten women who are married or living common law were physically abused.
The figures are staggering. The Vancouver police, when they formed their estimates in that city, said they receive, on average, 44 domestic calls about violence on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays, and that on other days in the week the average number of these calls is 38 a day. We know that more than twice as many women as men are murdered by members of their own families.
This incidence of violence is an issue which we simply cannot ignore, and that is why I am pleased to see that my colleague has brought it to the floor of the House this afternoon. It is an issue to which we must begin to give much more priority. We can begin that by asking the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs to look into this matter and recommend measures for the prevention, identification and treatment of victims of family violence.
Not enough is being done at the moment. For example, the transition houses, about which my hon. friend spoke, which give shelter to battered wives, are too few and are underfunded. About half the female population does not have ready access to transition houses, and those who do must qualify for welfare before they can get into a transitional house. I know
Family Violence
that from my own experience as a member of the board of directors of one such interval house in Kingston.
Women who are forced to flee to transition houses often have to do so in the middle of the night with scarcely more than the clothes on their backs. They are forced out into the cold, into the dark, as a result of severe physical abuse. According to statistics-and statistics can never tell the whole story-one out of every three such women has been beaten not just once or twice, but daily or weekly. They leave their homes in sheer desperation, and therefore the financial situation of the family of which they were once part, should not be a criterion for receiving financial assistance. For these women who are driven out, no matter what social background they come from, are truly destitute.
If this resolution is referred to committee, then the possibilities of preventive action could be investigated. Better educational and counselling programs could be recommended. Not just the general public, but police forces throughout the country, as the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) said, should become more sensitive to the problem.
It has been found that half the callers pleading for a police presence during husband and wife disputes were only given advice over the phone, but no physical protection. Couples should have better access to counselling, and the public should be made aware of the severity of the problem. Women should be encouraged to speak up and speak out if they are being abused. So many battered wives live in a world of private terror; they are afraid to stay and yet they are afraid to leave. These women must be provided with more financial and moral support than they have at present.
If this resolution is referred to the committee, it could also look into the legal aspects of wife battering to determine whether or not the laws on our books are adequate to protect wives who have been beaten and who are physically abused. For example, it could ask how effective restraining orders are. In a case study published last year by the Advisory Council on the Status of Women we were told of a woman, who, after she and her daughter had both been severely beaten by the husband, got the court to pass a restraining order on him. Not only did the restraining order not dissuade him from beating his wife again, nearly to the point of death, but when he was brought up on charges of attempted murder, he was given a suspended sentence for assault. He paid no fine, he spent no time in jail, but his wife still has the scars she received while he was under a restraining order.
Wife battering is, as has been said, a multidimensional problem, which calls for changes in the fields of law, education, medicine, social services, the economy and in the attitude of the public.
We must listen to what women have to say and we must be prepared to help. Indeed, sir, women are beginning to speak out more and more about this issue, in conferences, and in seminars across the country where they are meeting to discuss problems which women have in society. One such conference will be held here tomorrow, right on Parliament Hill, and I refer of course to the constitutional conference on women.

Hundreds of women from all across the country will be gathering together to discuss women's rights, family law, the role of the social services, women in employment and women in education. We in this chamber can do our part this afternoon by taking the resolution of my colleague seriously and referring it to committee instead of allowing it to be talked out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to speak to this motion. The Department of National Health and Welfare has been concerned for some time now with the prevention of family violence and countermeasures have been taken in that area. Several projects have been developed to help people take sound and positive life habits and thus avoid that kind of situation. For instance, a number of activities within the Health Protection Branch are aimed at fostering women's interest in their condition and keeping them well informed on their health and that of their family. An information kit on women and drug addiction has been developed, including a report on alcohol and violence. The Social Service Programs Branch is deeply concerned with family violence.
In the last three years the marriage counselling service has sponsored and Financed 20 symposia throughout Canada. These meetings of specialists in various branches reviewed the common aspects of family law and social services, particularly reform of family law, custody and visiting privileges, alimony payments, arbitration, counselling standards, legal procedures and the responsibility of the public and the specialists.
The report on abused and neglected children drafted by the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare led to the establishment of a plan of action at the ministerial level and to the creation of a position of co-ordinator for the information program on child abuse within the social services division which has begun to play an important role in the field of public teaching by co-ordinating and circulating information through films and printed matter.
Consultations have been undertaken with provincial authorities and private organizations to determine early detection methods, interdisciplinary measures and appropriate treatment so as to help the abused children and the people responsible for the abuse. In addition, the national welfare grants program has sponsored 14 projects on mistreated children since January 1977 and we have begun the last stage of a two-year study on basic legislative questions related to child abuse. The Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Justice have funded an exhaustive study on sexual offences against children and young people.
While continuing our efforts and supporting programs to fight child abuse we now consider that the most urgent aspect of family violence is the case of battered wives. Under the
department's two major grants programs, namely, the national welfare grants program and the national health research and development program, funds have been earmarked for over 40 pilot projects and research concerning family violence and sexual violence.
Through the Canada Assistance Plan we have paid for 50 per cent of services offered to neglected and mistreated children. Through that same plan we also share with the provinces half the cost of a great many financial and support services for victims of family violence. These funds help administer transition homes for battered wives.
We are also endeavouring, in concert with the Canadian Nurses' Association and the Canadian Association of Social Workers, to make the members of those two more aware of the problem of battered wives and inform them of the steps they can take. In fact, the social workers' association has set up a group of experts chaired by a department representative.
The problem is serious and far more widespread than anyone of us would dare admit. The efforts of the department are no more than a start and we are aware of it. The problem has now been identified but much remains to be done in determining the causes of wife battering and developing preventive measures, interdisciplinary services and appropriate care to help not only its victims but also those responsible for such ill treatment. We support whatever steps can contribute to educate the public and develop means to fight against the physical abuse of women; we therefore support the motion to refer the matter to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, Mr. Speaker.
