I also want to congratulate the various women's groups throughout the country which are working so hard to do something for battered wives in particular. In that connection I want to pay particular tribute to two groups in my own constituency of Moncton. There are two associations. One is called "Crossroads for Women". Its objective is to provide a shelter service for women who have been battered and abused, and to set up a referral service to aid women who are in crisis situations. The shelter or transition house which the association is trying to establish will accommodate women and their children. Also there is another project called "Project Aware". It is sponsored by the YWCA in Moncton. It provides access for women to assistance and resources to enable them to become self-sufficient. Both of these groups were to be funded under the Canada community services project. Unfortunately the money for that province ran out.
I have implored the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) to see if more money cannot be found somewhere for these worthy groups and their worthy projects. I am pleased to report that the minister is very sympathetic to my pleas and to these women in my riding. I trust the money will be forthcoming in the near future.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Island (Miss MacDonald) quite correctly said that statistics do not tell the whole story, but we need to hammer the facts of this story home by statistics. In 1978 an estimated 500,000 Canadian women or one in ten of those married or living common law were battered by the men with whom they lived.
Two thirds of all divorce applications are filed by women. More than one quarter of these divorces are requested on grounds that include physical cruelty. Eight out of ten of the women seeking shelter in a Canadian transition house have been beaten while they were pregnant. One of three residents in homes for battered women have been beaten weekly or daily. Those are frightening and shocking statistics.
The ramifications go beyond the beating of women and the beating of children. Fifteen per cent of Canadian police killed between 1961 and 1973 died while investigating domestic disputes. My colleague, the hon. member for York-Sunbury will recall a very tragic incident in the province of New Brunswick a few years ago in which two RCMP officers were killed in circumstances such as this. So the ramifications go beyond even the serious situation which we know exists in the homes of this country.
The government is most concerned about the reported increase in these statistics. On January 12, 1981, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) tabled Bill C-53 which contains
Family Violence
measures which would impose strict penalties for several of the problems associated with domestic or family violence. Such provisions resulted from careful study of the present legal sanctions within the federal sphere of responsibility and of the current use of these sanctions.
Pursuant to passage of clause 18, of Bill C-53, what is now called common assault, a summary conviction offence, will become what is referred to as a "hybrid" offence of assault. Under this hybrid offence, the Crown will elect whether to proceed by way of summary conviction where the maximum penalty is six months and/or a $500 fine, or by indictment where the maximum penalty would be two years' imprisonment. Because the offence is hybrid, the police will be able to arrest an assailant without actually finding that person committing an assault. This is terribly important, as the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands has pointed out. The police will operate on the belief that it is in the best interest of the public to take the assailant into custody in cases were they have reasonable and probable grounds to believe the offence is likely to be repeated.
This will be especially helpful in cases of wife battering where the police may be called by a neighbour. Their arrival on the scene usually stops the beating. At the present, unless the wife has sustained injuries sufficient to constitute the offence of assault causing bodily harm, the police are unable to arrest unless they actually see the assault occurring. This, of course, is rarely the case. As a result, where the wife does not seek shelter away from the house and the husband is not arrested, frequently when the police leave the scene, notwithstanding that they believe the tension has been defused, the wife is again beaten by the husband.
This amendment to the assault section of the Criminal Code will provide a tool to the police to arrest without actually seeing the assault. Their judgment in assessing each situation becomes all important, and we can only hope that individual police departments will ensure that officers answering domestic calls will receive specialized training. To this end, federal and provincial police forces are working together to develop such police training.
Of course, once an arrest is made, the prosecution of a case falls within the responsibility of a provincial Crown attorney. There is some dispute about whether such matters ought to be dealt with in family court or in criminal court. The legal forum in which a case is presented often depends on the local situation regarding such things as the availability of court time, the availability of a prosecutor, and the procedures established by the local judges and so on.
However, the federal Department of Justice has awarded research and demonstration grants to obtain further information on the legal process in such cases and to assist complainants in the court process. For example, the Women's Research Centre in Vancouver is preparing a report on the legal process, and a demonstration project for a complainant consultant is under consideration for Windsor, Ontario. Under this project information would be provided to those assaulted in domestic situations about their legal rights and this would

further assist those victims who proceed with assault charges as they move through the court process, whether in family court or in criminal court. It is anticipated this project will assist the Crown attorneys in processing these cases brought before the courts.
In relation to the abuse of children, the Minister of Justice announced, in co-operation with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), that a national study would be established under the chairmanship of Dr. Robin Badgely on the sexual abuse of children. The study is expected to last two years. In addition, the federal government, in conjunction with the province of Nova Scotia, is funding a study on child abuse. Also, in Clause 6 of Bill C-53, serious responsibilities and sanctions are imposed on parents, guardians and others in authority not to molest their charges or permit them to engage in sexual misconduct.
As it has been demonstrated that the rules of evidence need to be amended to permit one spouse to be compellable and compellent to give evidence against the other spouse in child abuse cases, the necessary amendment to the Evidence Act is proposed in Bill C-53. These legislative measures are the one
area within the federal sphere of responsibility involving domestic violence where the federal government can take immediate action.
Notwithstanding these current initiatives the government supports further study and action and would welcome the assistance of the Standing Committe on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. Therefore, in concluding this debate, I am pleased to indicate that the Government of Canada supports the motion of the hon. member for York-Sunbury.
